text.p: Russian oil producer Chernogorneft said on Tuesday it achieved profit before tax of $37.4 million in the first half of this year on net sales of $264.9 million.
The unaudited figures are to the new accruals-based Russian accounting standards, so comparisons are not available.
According to the old cash-based accounting standards, pre-tax profit fell to $19.4 million in the first half of this year from $29.4 million in the same 1995 period.
Chernogorneft said it has also prepared first half figures audited by Ernst and Young to U.S. GAAP standards, but these have not yet been published.

NOTES - Average exchange rate in first half 1996 is 4,894 roubles per dollar. Exchange rate at end of period 5,108, at start of period 4,640. Shareholders' equity, receivables and accounts payable as of July 1.

Total output includes output from three joint ventures and production-sharing agreements with local service companies. Reserves are annual audit by Miller and Lents less period's output. Oil sales represent only oil actually paid for, not total deliveries.

Full name AOOT Chernogorneft. NK Sidanko owns 37.7 percent, and Uneximbank (Oneksimbank in Russian) and affiliates Bank ICFI (MFK Bank) and Moscow Partners own 17.3 percent. Another 14.9 percent of shares are held in American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) through Bank of New York, and 8.1 percent in Russian Depositary Receipts through ING Barings. Other foreign entities own 11.6 percent, with five foreign entities holding over one percent each, individual shareholders own 7.8 percent and other Russian entities 2.5 percent.

The Uneximbank group has control over Chernogorneft, as MFK Bank backed by Uneximbank won control of 51 percent of Sidanko under the government's shares-for-loans programme. Earlier this month Interros Oil acquired 34 percent of Sidanko at an investment tender. The Interros group includes Uneximbank and MFK Bank. Under the terms of the tender for Sidanko, the winner must transfer to Sidanko at least 13 percent of Chernogorneft.

These figures are not prepared to international accounting standards but to Russian accounting standards, which differ significantly from those normally supplied in the West. Russian accounts are designed to meet the requirements of the tax authorities. Definitions of profit and assets differ significantly from those in the West, and converting Russian accounts to international standards can turn a profit into a loss.
